🚨🛫 BREAKING: The Premier League have released the VAR conversation between Michael Oliver and the VAR officials during the controversial Morgan Rogers handball incident against Chelsea.

The audio reveals VAR disagreed with the penalty decision, but Oliver stood by his call.

🚨THE AUDIO: 

VAR 1: Michael, we're checking the possible handball involving Morgan Rogers. Just hold the restart for now.

Michael Oliver: Okay. What's the situation?

VAR 1: We're checking the contact between the ball and Rogers' upper body. We need to establish whether there's contact with the arm.

VAR 2: Can we have the side angle, please?

VAR 3: I've got it. Let's slow that down.

VAR 1: Looking at the footage, the ball appears to make contact with the top of his shoulder before travelling towards his face.

Michael Oliver: Are you sure that's the first point of contact?

VAR 2: Yes, Michael. Watch it again. The ball hits the upper shoulder first, then changes direction towards his face.

VAR 1: Can we have another angle? I want to check whether there's any contact with the arm afterwards.

VAR 3: I've checked the reverse angle. I can't identify any clear contact with the arm. The initial contact is above the sleeve line.

Michael Oliver: But his arm is away from his body. That's what I'm looking at.

VAR 1: We understand, but we're trying to establish whether the ball actually makes contact with his arm. The footage currently shows shoulder contact.

VAR 2: I agree. His arm position might look unusual at normal speed, but the ball doesn't appear to hit it.

VAR 3: Michael, I think you should have a look at the monitor. The side angle is quite clear.

Michael Oliver: Send it through.

VAR 1: Sending now. This is the front angle at normal speed. Now we're slowing it down.

Michael Oliver: Okay.

VAR 1: Watch the ball closely. It makes contact with the top of Rogers' shoulder before going towards his face.

VAR 2: Exactly. That's the important part of the incident. We're not seeing a clear contact with the arm.

Michael Oliver: I still think his arm is in an unnatural position.

VAR 1: Michael, can we show you the side angle once more? It gives a much clearer picture of the contact.

VAR 3: Here it is. Shoulder first, then face. We have reviewed the available angles and cannot establish a clear handball offence.

Michael Oliver: I understand what you're saying, but for me, the arm position is the issue.

VAR 2: But the ball appears to hit his shoulder. We don't have evidence that it makes contact with the arm.

VAR 1: Michael, our recommendation is that you reconsider the decision. We believe the footage does not support a clear handball offence.

Michael Oliver: I've looked at all the angles. I'm satisfied with what I've seen.

VAR 3: Just to be clear, are you maintaining the penalty decision?

Michael Oliver: Yes. For me, it's a penalty. His arm is in an unnatural position, and I'm not changing my decision.

VAR 1: Michael, one final time, the ball makes contact with the top of his shoulder before his face. We cannot identify clear arm contact.

Michael Oliver: I hear you, but I've made my decision. Penalty to Leeds.

VAR 2: Understood. On-field decision stands.

VAR 3: Check complete.

VAR 1: Penalty confirmed.

Michael Oliver: Thank you. Check over now. Let's restart.

VAR 2: Copy that.

Michael Oliver: Let's move on.

END OF AUDIO.

Last Tuesday, a man came through the doors of the county animal shelter where I work, yanking a trembling chocolate-brown Boxer mix named Milo along behind him.

“Take him back,” the man snapped. “He bit me. That dog’s dangerous. You ought to put him to sleep.”

We moved Milo to a quarantine kennel. He tucked himself into the farthest corner, shivering so hard I could see it from the doorway. His food sat untouched. Everyone on staff knew how much harder things could get for a dog once a bite went on his record.

On Thursday, just after we unlocked the doors, a woman came in wearing dark glasses. They barely hid the bruise across her cheek. Her hands shook as she asked if we still had Milo.

I said we did and gently explained what the man had reported and what it might mean for him. She started to cry before I could finish.

“My husband had me pinned down,” she told me. “Milo caught him by the arm. That’s how I got away.”

Standing there listening to her, I understood why her husband had sounded so angry when he brought Milo in. He wanted the dog punished for getting between them.

I took my keys and went straight back for him. The instant Milo saw her, he let out a cry that carried across the room. He scrambled over the floor to reach her and pressed himself against her, both front paws wrapped around her as if he couldn’t bear to let go.

That afternoon, she loaded up her car and drove out of state with Milo beside her.

The bite report said what Milo had done. She was the one who could tell us why. When she needed a way out, he gave her one.

Denmark's Supreme Court rules that landlords of social housing estates don’t engage in illegal ethnic discrimination when they evict “non-Western' tenants.”

The Supreme Court says the “non-Western”!criterion is neutral.

The court’s ruling is a major win for Danish political parties who are working to rid the country of “migrant ghettos.”

Seven families from Helsingor, north of Copenhagen, had their leases terminated in 2022 under a 2018 law.

This law states that all social housing estates where more than half of residents are “non-Western” must rebuild, renovate and change the social mix by renting at least 60 per cent of the homes at market rates by 2030.

The law is aimed at combating segregation and “parallel societies” in disadvantaged neighbourhoods.

“Non-Western” is one criterion the Danish government uses to define “transformation areas”, which it previously termed “hard ghettos.”

In Helsingor, the landlord Boliggarden announced in early 2020 that it would carry out extensive renovations on seven stairwells - 96 apartments in total.

It terminated the leases of those tenants, most of whom were of foreign origin.
Seven families argued they had been discriminated against based on ethnic origin and took legal action.
￼
The Danish Supreme Court has now ruled that it wasn’t ethnic discrimination.
￼
Some 11,000 people across Denmark will have to leave their apartments to be rehoused elsewhere by 2030 to comply with the 2018 law.

According to Denmark's definition, “non-Western” countries include every country in the world except the 27 member states of the European Union, as well as Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the Vatican, Canada, the United Kingdom, The United States, Australia and New Zealand.

The Fed could be much closer to ending its rate hikes than most people think.

Before the September hike, US Treasury yields kept going up. The 10-year yield hit 5.23%, its highest level since 2007.

That was the bond market telling the Fed to raise rates, and the Fed did.

Now the bond market is saying something different.

The Fed hiked in September and paused in October, and markets see about a 100% chance of another hike in December.

But yields are falling anyway:

- 2-year yield: 4.83% → 4.68%
- 10-year yield: 5.12% → 4.9%

The 2-year yield matters most, because it moves with where traders think Fed rates are going.

If the Fed hikes in December, its rate goes to 4.00–4.25%.

With the 2-year at 4.68% and dropping, markets are pricing very little hiking after that.

The reason is simple.

Rates are already at their highest level in years, and the stock market just had its worst week in years.

The more the Fed pushes from here, the bigger the risk that something in the economy breaks.

Inflation is also starting to cool. 

Oil has dropped about 18% this month.

Because of that, prediction markets expect November CPI to come in at -0.1%. 

That means prices would fall for the month.

That CPI report comes on Dec 10, one day after the Fed meets. 

So the Fed may still hike in December, but the data after that could give it a clear reason to stop.

If the Fed is forced to stop earlier than expected, it would be a big bullish catalyst for Bitcoin and other risk assets.

But inflation is still the main risk. If oil bounces back or CPI comes in hot, the case for more hikes returns, and yields can go right back up.
